summary: Gives a fuller specification of the file URI scheme, replacing the short definition in RFC 1738, with a common syntax across existing usage and notes on current practices.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC fixes the exact spelling of the addresses that point at files on a computer, so that two programs agree on what "file:///etc/hosts" means, what a host name in front of it means, and how unusual characters in a file name are escaped.

questions: how to write a file url
subtitle: The precise syntax for file: URIs, replacing the one-paragraph definition in RFC 1738.

tldr.problem: The file URI scheme had been defined only by a paragraph in RFC 1738, which predated the generic URI syntax, so it left several parts of the scheme underspecified and different implementations disagreed about them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC derives the scheme from the generic syntax of RFC 3986, defines it in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, and explains what local and non-local file URIs mean, how file names are encoded, and how the scheme is registered with IANA.
tldr.outcome: The result is one agreed spelling for file addresses, covering the three forms in common use. RFC 8089 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1738, and it was itself updated by RFC 9844.

today: RFC 8089 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1738, and it was itself updated by RFC 9844. It is the definition of the file URI scheme registered with IANA.

sections.title: What a File URI Is
sections.content:
A file URI identifies an object, a "file", stored in a structured object naming and accessing environment on a host, which is to say a file system. The URI can be used in discussions about the file, and if other conditions are met it can be dereferenced to access the file directly.

This document specifies a syntax based on the generic syntax of RFC 3986 that is compatible with most existing usages. Where incompatibilities arise, they are usually in parts of the scheme that were underspecified in earlier definitions and have been tightened up by more recent specifications.

Extensions to the syntax that might be encountered in practice are listed in Appendix E, for information only; they are not a requirement of implementation. The file URI scheme is not coupled with a specific protocol, nor with a specific media type.

Two terms carry weight throughout the document. A "local file" is a file that can be accessed through the local file system API using only the information included in the file path, not relying on other information such as network addresses. A local file may not be physically located on the local machine, for example if a networked file system is transparently mounted into the local file system. A "local file URI" is a file URI that has no authority component, or where the authority is the special string "localhost" or a fully qualified domain name that resolves to the machine from which the URI is being interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC fixes the exact spelling of the addresses that point at files, so that two programs agree on what "file:///etc/hosts" means.

sections.title: The Syntax
sections.content:
The file URI syntax is defined in Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF), importing the "host" and "path-absolute" rules from RFC 3986 as updated by RFC 6874. The generic syntax in RFC 3986 includes "path" and "authority" components, and for each of them only a subset is used here: the relevant subset of "path" is "path-absolute", and the subset of "authority" is "file-auth".

The definition differs from those in RFC 1630 and RFC 1738, because it is derived from the generic syntax of RFC 3986, which postdates the previous file URI specifications.

The rules themselves are short. A file URI is a scheme, a colon, and then either an authority followed by an absolute path, or just an absolute path. The authority is either the literal string "localhost" or a host name.

The "host" is the fully qualified domain name of the system on which the file is accessible. That allows a client on another system to know that it cannot access the file system, or perhaps that it needs to use some other local mechanism to access the file. As a special case, "localhost" is interpreted as "the machine from which the URI is being interpreted", exactly as if no authority were present.

The RFC notes that current usage disagrees about this. Some implementations incorrectly interpret all values in the authority of a file URI, including "localhost", as non-local. Others interpret any value as local, even if the host does not resolve to the local machine. To maximize compatibility with previous specifications, users MAY choose to include an auth-path with no file-auth when creating a URI.

The path component is the absolute path to the file in the file system. Some file systems have case-sensitive file naming and some do not, so the scheme supports case sensitivity in order to retain the case as given. Any transport-related handling of the file URI scheme MUST retain the case as given, and any mapping to or from a case-insensitive form is solely the responsibility of the implementation processing the URI on behalf of the referenced file system.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three shapes: no host at all, the word "localhost", or a real host name. The path always starts with a slash, and the case of the letters is preserved exactly as written.

sections.title: Operations on File URIs
sections.content:
A file URI can be dependably dereferenced or translated to a local file path only if it is local. A file URI is considered local if it has no file-auth, or the file-auth is the special string "localhost", or a fully qualified domain name that resolves to the machine from which the URI is being interpreted. This specification neither defines nor forbids any set of operations that might be performed on a file identified by a non-local file URI. The POSIX file and directory operations give examples of standardized operations that can be performed on files.

Appendix D gathers system-specific guidance that is not normative. On POSIX systems the root of the file system is a directory with a zero-length name, usually written as "/", and its presence in a file URI can be taken as given by the initial slash in the path-absolute rule. Common UNIX shells such as bash and zsh provide a function known as "tilde expansion", where a path that begins with a tilde can be expanded out to a special directory name; no such facility exists using the file URI scheme, so a tilde in a file URI is always just a tilde.

When mapping a DOS- or Windows-like file path to a file URI, the drive letter is typically mapped into the first path segment. The Hierarchical File System Plus on Mac OS X uses a nonstandard normalization form, similar to Normalization Form D, so care is needed when transforming paths to and from URIs. On OpenVMS Files-11 systems the device name is mapped into the first path segment, the dollar sign is a reserved character under the definition in RFC 3986 and should be percent-encoded if present in the device name, and a node reference included in the path is used as the authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a local file URI can safely be turned into a file path. The appendix also notes the quirks: a tilde is just a tilde here, and on Windows the drive letter becomes the first folder name.

sections.title: File System Name Encoding
sections.content:
File systems use various encoding schemes to store file and directory names. Many modern file systems store file and directory names as arbitrary sequences of octets, in which case the representation as an encoded string often depends on the user's localization settings, or defaults to UTF-8.

When a file URI is produced that represents textual data consisting of characters from the Unicode Standard coded character set, the data SHOULD be encoded as octets according to the UTF-8 character encoding scheme before percent-encoding is applied, as per Section 2.5 of RFC 3986. A decision not to use percent-encoded UTF-8 is outside the scope of this specification. It will typically require the use of heuristics, or explicit knowledge about the way the string will be processed.
sections.plainLanguage: File names are turned into text by converting them to UTF-8 first and then escaping the characters that would not survive in a URL. Choosing anything else needs extra care.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are many security considerations for URI schemes discussed in RFC 3986. File access and the granting of privileges for specific operations are complex topics, and the use of file URIs can complicate the security model in effect for file privileges.

Historically, user agents have granted content from the file URI scheme a tremendous amount of privilege. However, granting all local files such wide privileges can lead to privilege escalation attacks. Some user agents have had success granting local files directory-based privileges, but this approach has not been widely adopted. Other user agents use globally unique identifiers as the origin for each file URI, which is the most secure option.

Treating a non-local file URI as local, or otherwise attempting to perform local operations on a non-local URI, can result in security problems.

File systems typically assign an operational meaning to special characters such as "/", "\", ":", "[" and "]", and to special device names like ".", "..", "...", "aux" and "lpt". In some cases, merely testing for the existence of such a name will cause the operating system to pause or invoke unrelated system calls, leading to significant security concerns regarding denial of service and unintended data transfer. It would not be possible for this specification to list all such significant characters and device names. Implementers should research the reserved names and characters for the types of storage devices that may be attached to their application and restrict the use of data obtained from URI components accordingly.

File systems also vary in the way they handle case. Care must be taken to avoid issues resulting from possibly unexpected aliasing from case-only differences between file paths or URIs, or from mismatched encodings or Unicode equivalences.
sections.plainLanguage: A file address is a powerful thing to hand to a program, because programs have long given local files wide access. The RFC also warns that names like ".." or "aux" mean something special to the operating system and must be handled carefully.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document defines the permanent URI scheme "file" and updates the "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes" registry accordingly. The registration complies with BCP 35. The applications and protocols that use the scheme name are described as commonly used in hypertext documents to refer to files without depending on network access, and supported by major browsers. It is also used in development libraries, such as the Windows Shell functions PathCreateFromUrl and UrlCreateFromPath, and the libwww-perl World-Wide Web library for Perl. The contact is the Applications and Real-Time Area, the change controller is the IETF, and the reference is this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of URI schemes, and this RFC records "file" there as a permanent scheme, with the IETF in charge of it.

sections.title: Example URIs
sections.content:
Appendix B gives the forms the syntax is intended to support. For local files there is the traditional file URI for a local file with an empty authority, which is the most common format in use today: "file:///path/to/file". There is also the minimal representation of a local file with no authority field and an absolute path that begins with a slash: "file:/path/to/file". For non-local files there is the form with an explicit authority: "file://host.example.com/path/to/file".

Appendix A records the significant difference from the earlier definitions. According to RFC 1738, a file URL always started with the token "file://", followed by an optionally blank host name and a "/". The syntax in this document makes the entire authority component, including the double slashes, optional.

Appendix C notes two similar technologies. The WHATWG URL specification defines browser behaviour for a variety of inputs, including file URIs; as a living document it changes to reflect updates in browser behaviour, so its algorithms and syntax definitions may or may not be consistent with this specification, and implementors should be aware of the possible discrepancy. The Universal Naming Convention defines a string format that can perform a similar role to the file URI scheme in describing the location of files, except that files located by UNC filespace selector strings are typically stored on a remote machine and accessed using a network protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Three forms cover nearly everything: a triple slash for a local file, a single slash for the same thing written briefly, and a host name for a file on another machine.

viz.caption: THE FILE URI SYNTAX, VERBATIM FROM RFC 8089

data.title: The file URI scheme
data.code:
file-URI       = file-scheme ":" file-hier-part

file-scheme    = "file"

file-hier-part = ( "//" auth-path )
               / local-path

auth-path      = [ file-auth ] path-absolute

local-path     = path-absolute

file-auth      = "localhost"
               / host

viz.caption: THE THREE FILE URI FORMS FROM APPENDIX B

items.text: The file system root is the initial slash. A tilde in a URI is always just a tilde.

items.title: Mac OS X
items.text: HFS+ uses a nonstandard normalization form, so take care when converting paths.

items.title: OpenVMS
items.text: The device name maps into the first path segment, and a node reference becomes the authority.
